reviewScope: Black Whale vessel, spatial, access, operational, structural and scale evidence only

pass1.method: Full-page visual sweep of all 19 ordered pages

pass2.method: Full-resolution inspection of the retained page and exterior panel

retainedPanels.subject: Pre-launch promotional exterior reveal of Black Whale No. 1 in a harbor
retainedPanels.visualDescription: A colossal whale-shaped transport vessel dominates a harbor. The visible concept has a black hemispherical upper body, a pale lower hull, a whale eye and ribbed mouth treatment, a circular recessed top deck with a central structure, and a rectangular projection or ramp on the near-facing flank. Small boats, an airship, waterfront buildings and port infrastructure provide scale cues.
modelingPermissions: Use as an early macro-silhouette reference
Record the visible exterior feature inventory
Use surrounding harbor objects only for broad scale class
modelingProhibitions: Do not derive exact metric dimensions
Do not assign port, starboard, bow-axis coordinates from panel direction alone
Do not treat this promotional design as the final launched geometry without later corroboration
Do not infer unseen interior layout from the exterior shell

evidence.claim: The vessel is publicly introduced as the giant transport ship Black Whale No. 1 with a stated capacity of 200,000 people.
evidence.modelingUse: Occupancy class and programme-scale constraint; not a usable floor-area calculation by itself.

evidence.claim: The promotional presentation describes the interior design as simplified for transport use.
evidence.modelingUse: Supports utilitarian mass-transport language outside elite zones; does not define a room plan.

evidence.claim: The presentation links the simplified transport design to lower cost and faster construction.
evidence.modelingUse: Supports repetitive, economical construction assumptions only when later visual evidence agrees.

evidence.claim: Kakin publicly announces a plan to produce twenty similar ships within one year.
evidence.modelingUse: Programme context only; no direct geometry permission.

evidence.claim: The presentation states a five-year ambition to send 100 million people toward the Dark Continent programme.
evidence.modelingUse: Operational context only; no direct geometry permission.

evidence.claim: The first ship is presented as carrying Beyond, the Kakin king and all fourteen princes.
evidence.modelingUse: Supports the presence of distinct expedition leadership and royal accommodation classes.

evidence.claim: General passengers are to be selected by lottery, with the presentation stating a one-in-1,300 chance of receiving a ticket for the first ship.
evidence.modelingUse: Supports controlled mass-passenger access and ticketed boarding operations.

evidence.claim: The promotional exterior concept shows a black hemispherical upper body over a pale lower hull with a whale eye and ribbed mouth treatment.
evidence.modelingUse: Early concept silhouette only, pending comparison with launched-vessel panels.

evidence.claim: The visible concept includes a circular recessed top deck with a central structure and a rectangular projection or ramp on the near-facing flank.
evidence.modelingUse: Feature inventory; exact function and later continuity remain unresolved.

evidence.claim: The vessel is depicted as vastly larger than nearby boats, an airship and surrounding harbor districts.
evidence.modelingUse: Broad colossal scale class only; perspective prevents metric extraction.

contradictionsAndQuarantines.subject: Promotional concept versus launched vessel
contradictionsAndQuarantines.rule: Chapter 342 exterior features remain early-concept evidence until compared against later exterior panels. Later launched-vessel evidence controls final geometry when conflict exists.

unresolvedQuestions: Does the circular recessed top structure correspond to the later Tier 1 cruise-ship zone or an abandoned early design?
Is the near-facing rectangular projection a boarding ramp, cargo ramp, tender dock or another access mechanism?
Which visible end is the canonical bow cannot be assigned solely from panel orientation, despite the whale-face motif.
